goals: Characterize how modeled peak SWE varies across the Wenatchee elevation gradient (187-2870 m)
Validate modeled peak SWE against 5 SNOTEL stations
key_processes: orographic precipitation and temperature partitioning of snow vs rain

model_choice.rationale: Single-column ELM natively simulates snow/SWE (H2OSNO, QSNOMELT, SNOW) and, with NLDAS-2 CONUS forcing, resolves elevation-dependent precip/temperature across the basin. No lateral processes required for a peak-SWE question.

answerable: Direction and gross shape of the peak-SWE vs elevation relationship, since NLDAS-2 forcing varies precip/temperature with location and elevation across CONUS
Co-located comparison of modeled peak SWE to the 5 SNOTEL stations (SWE is in default history output)

not_answerable.why: NLDAS-2 at ~12 km cannot resolve sub-12 km terrain; a single cell averages over ~2683 m of relief, so no within-cell lapse rate and ridgetop SWE is underestimated (expected bias at SNOTEL sites)

sampling_strategy.approach: stratified by elevation, plus observation-pinned validation columns
sampling_strategy.n_justification: One column per elevation band (6 bands spanning 187-2870 m) resolves the SWE-elevation curve including the rain-snow transition, without a dense blind grid. Elevation is the only candidate driver, so replication across bands is prioritized over within-band replication.
sampling_strategy.placement_logic: Concentrate columns to span the full relief with tighter spacing around the rain-snow transition (600-1600 m) where peak SWE is most sensitive to the snow/rain partition; ensure at least one column in the alpine band to expose the expected NLDAS underestimation.
sampling_strategy.replication: None within bands; the 5 SNOTEL-pinned validation columns provide additional real-world anchoring at their elevations.

sampling_plan.reason: Anchors the low-SWE end of the gradient where precipitation falls mostly as rain.
Captures the elevation where peak SWE is most sensitive to the rain/snow partition.
Resolves the steep rise of peak SWE with elevation.
Mid-upper band where SNOTEL stations typically sit; core of the accumulation zone.
Upper accumulation zone; tests peak-SWE magnitude before terrain-averaging bias dominates.
Exposes the expected NLDAS ridgetop underestimation at the top of the gradient.
Co-located with the 5 SNOTEL stations to compare modeled vs observed peak SWE directly.

validation_design.comparison: co-located - place a column at each SNOTEL station's nearest NLDAS cell and compare annual peak SWE and its timing over overlapping years
validation_design.metric: bias, RMSE, and correlation of annual peak SWE; expect low bias amplified at higher-elevation stations

experiment_summary.primary_treatment: NLDAS-2 forcing, native SSURGO soil, short lead-in to settle states

requires_capabilities.why: NLDAS-2 at ~12 km cannot resolve within-cell lapse rate over 2683 m of relief
requires_capabilities.blocks: accurate high-elevation/ridgetop peak-SWE magnitude and unbiased SNOTEL comparison at ridge sites

requires_capabilities.why: needed to extract annual peak SWE per column
requires_capabilities.blocks: both the gradient characterization and SNOTEL validation (available by default)

requires_capabilities.why: downstream expander must place columns into elevation bands from a real DEM
to pin validation columns and load observed peak SWE
to constrain sampling to the Wenatchee basin

assumptions: Wenatchee (HUC 17020011) lies within CONUS NLDAS-2 coverage, so elevation-dependent forcing is available.
SNOTEL stations fall within the basin and have SWE records overlapping 1980-2018.
Peak SWE is a fast (annual) state, so multi-year water-table spin-up is unnecessary; a short lead-in suffices.
SSURGO soil is available per column; soil is held at native values since elevation is the only driver of interest.
open_questions: Which years should the SWE climatology cover (full 1980-2018 vs a recent subset), and should we report multi-year mean peak SWE or per-year?
What are the actual elevations of the 5 SNOTEL stations, to confirm they span the upper bands where bias is expected?
Is snow-course data truly unavailable, or could any be obtained to check mid-slope/off-station elevations?
